tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Give helper functions a new Verb-Noun name such as Read-Doc, also in script files. A built-in alias (rd, rm, del, ri, sc, mv and others) runs instead of a function with the same name, with no warning.
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
    - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. A call a usage limit refused, or one still running when the run stopped, usually runs again without ending reuse: finished calls after it still come from cache. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

    """Write UTF-8 Markdown without overwriting; returns the path actually written."""
    target = Path(path)

def _pe_metadata(data: bytes) -> Optional[dict]:
    if len(data) < 64 or data[:2] != b"MZ":
        return None
    pe_offset = struct.unpack_from("<I", data, 0x3C)[0]
    if pe_offset + 24 > len(data) or data[pe_offset:pe_offset + 4] != b"PE\0\0":
        return None
    optional = pe_offset + 24
    magic = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, optional)[0]
    is_64 = magic == 0x20B
    if magic not in (0x10B, 0x20B):
        return None
    entry_rva = struct.unpack_from("<I", data, optional + 16)[0]
    image_base = struct.unpack_from("<Q" if is_64 else "<I", data, optional + (24 if is_64 else 28))[0]
    directory_count_offset = optional + (108 if is_64 else 92)
    directory_offset = optional + (112 if is_64 else 96)
    signed = False
    if directory_count_offset + 4 <= len(data) and struct.unpack_from("<I", data, directory_count_offset)[0] > 4:
        certificate = directory_offset + 4 * 8
        if certificate + 8 <= len(data):
            signed = struct.unpack_from("<II", data, certificate) != (0, 0)
    return {"rva": entry_rva, "image_base": image_base, "signed": signed, "is_64": is_64}

def save_report(markdown: str, path: Path) -> Path:
    """Write UTF-8 Markdown without overwriting; returns the path actually written."""
    target = Path(path)

    candidate = target
    counter = 2
    while candidate.exists():
        candidate = target.with_name("{0}_{1}{2}".format(target.stem, counter, target.suffix))
        counter += 1
    with open(candidate, "x", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        handle.write(markdown)

192	def _sample_metadata(path: Optional[str], triage: Mapping[str, Any]) -> dict:
193	    file_type = triage.get("file_type") or "Unknown"
194	    architecture = triage.get("architecture") or "Unknown"
195	    meta = {"File type": str(file_type), "Architecture": str(architecture), "File size": "Unavailable",
196	            "Entry point": "Unavailable", "SHA256": "Unavailable", "Digital signature": "Unknown"}
197	    if not path:
198	        return meta
199	    try:
200	        target = Path(path)
201	        size = target.stat().st_size
202	        meta["File size"] = "{0} bytes".format(size)
203	        digest = hashlib.sha256()
204	        with target.open("rb") as handle:
205	            for block in iter(lambda: handle.read(1024 * 1024), b""):
206	                digest.update(block)
207	        meta["SHA256"] = digest.hexdigest()
208	        with target.open("rb") as handle:
209	            header = handle.read(4096)
210	        pe = _pe_metadata(header)
211	        if pe:
212	            meta["Entry point"] = "RVA {0} / VA {1}".format(_hex(pe["rva"]), _hex(pe["image_base"] + pe["rva"]))
213	            meta["Digital signature"] = "Signed (certificate present; validity not verified)" if pe["signed"] else "Unsigned"
214	            if str(file_type).lower() == "unknown":
215	                meta["File type"] = "PE32+ EXE" if pe["is_64"] else "PE32 EXE"
216	            if str(architecture).lower() == "unknown":
217	                meta["Architecture"] = "x64" if pe["is_64"] else "x86"
218	        return meta
219	    except (OSError, ValueError, struct.error):
220	        return meta

223	def _pe_metadata(data: bytes) -> Optional[dict]:
224	    if len(data) < 64 or data[:2] != b"MZ":
225	        return None
226	    pe_offset = struct.unpack_from("<I", data, 0x3C)[0]
227	    if pe_offset + 24 > len(data) or data[pe_offset:pe_offset + 4] != b"PE\0\0":
228	        return None
229	    optional = pe_offset + 24
230	    magic = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, optional)[0]
231	    is_64 = magic == 0x20B
232	    if magic not in (0x10B, 0x20B):
233	        return None
234	    entry_rva = struct.unpack_from("<I", data, optional + 16)[0]
235	    image_base = struct.unpack_from("<Q" if is_64 else "<I", data, optional + (24 if is_64 else 28))[0]
236	    directory_count_offset = optional + (108 if is_64 else 92)
237	    directory_offset = optional + (112 if is_64 else 96)
238	    signed = False
239	    if directory_count_offset + 4 <= len(data) and struct.unpack_from("<I", data, directory_count_offset)[0] > 4:
240	        certificate = directory_offset + 4 * 8
241	        if certificate + 8 <= len(data):
242	            signed = struct.unpack_from("<II", data, certificate) != (0, 0)
243	    return {"rva": entry_rva, "image_base": image_base, "signed": signed, "is_64": is_64}

        FAIL.append(m)

    results[key] = (facts, findings)

    print(key, os.path.basename(path))
    print(format_static_facts(facts, findings))

if have("F50AD55F"):
    check(any("UPX" in w for w in results["F50AD55F"][0].wrappers), "F50A: UPX marker")
if have("5C28A30E", "95EFD543"):

          "no side-loading false positive on Unity/CODESYS")
print("\n{0} failure(s)".format(len(FAIL)))
sys.exit(1 if FAIL else 0)

    env = dict(os.environ, PYTHONIOENCODING="utf-8", PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1")
    failed = []
    for suite in suites:
        name = os.path.basename(suite)[:-3]
        started = time.monotonic()
        proc = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-B", suite], cwd=HERE, env=env,
                              stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True, encoding="utf-8")
        tail = [line for line in proc.stdout.splitlines() if line.strip()][-1:] or ["(no output)"]

    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":

"""Offline test runner: no IDA, no network, no model calls.

    python tests/run_tests.py            # all suites
    python tests/run_tests.py verdict    # suites whose name contains "verdict"

Real-sample checks run only when IDA_AI_SAMPLES_DIR points at read-only sample copies.
"""
import glob
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import time

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))


def main(argv):
    selectors = [a.lower() for a in argv[1:]]
    suites = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(HERE, "test_*.py")))
    if selectors:
        suites = [s for s in suites if any(sel in os.path.basename(s).lower() for sel in selectors)]
    env = dict(os.environ, PYTHONIOENCODING="utf-8", PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1")
    failed = []
    for suite in suites:
        name = os.path.basename(suite)[:-3]
        started = time.monotonic()
        proc = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-B", suite], cwd=HERE, env=env,
                              stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True, encoding="utf-8")
        tail = [line for line in proc.stdout.splitlines() if line.strip()][-1:] or ["(no output)"]
        ok = proc.returncode == 0 and "FAIL" not in "\n".join(l for l in proc.stdout.splitlines() if l.startswith("FAIL"))
        print("{0:<6} {1:<22} {2:5.1f}s  {3}".format("ok" if ok else "FAILED", name, time.monotonic() - started, tail[0].strip()))
        if not ok:
            failed.append(name)
            print("\n".join("    " + l for l in proc.stdout.splitlines() if l.startswith("FAIL") or "Error" in l)[:4000])
    print("\n{0} suite(s), {1} failed{2}".format(len(suites), len(failed), (": " + ", ".join(failed)) if failed else ""))
    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv))

"""IDA entry point for the IDA AI Malware Analyst plugin.

This file is the only module IDA loads from its ``plugins`` directory. It
locates the plugin package and support files in one of two layouts and has no
AI or network behaviour of its own.

Release layout (what ``scripts/build_release.py`` produces and what an analyst
copies into IDA's ``plugins`` directory)::

    plugins/
      ida_ai_malware_analyst.py                 <- this file
      ida_ai_malware_analyst/                   <- plugin root
        ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin/          <- the package
        prompts/
        ida_ai_malware_analyst.json             <- optional local configuration

Development layout (this repository)::

    <repo>/
      ida_ai_malware_analyst.py                 <- this file; repo root is the plugin root
      src/ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin/
      prompts/
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Tuple


RELEASE_FOLDER_NAME = "ida_ai_malware_analyst"
PACKAGE_NAME = "ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin"


def resolve_layout(here: Path) -> Tuple[Path, Path]:
    """Return ``(plugin_root, package_dir)`` for the directory containing this file.

    ``plugin_root`` holds ``prompts/`` and the optional configuration file;
    ``package_dir`` is the ``sys.path`` entry that contains the package.
    Candidates, in order: the development layout (``<here>/src``), then the
    release layout (``<here>/ida_ai_malware_analyst/``). When neither exists the
    directory itself is used so a flat copy still imports.
    """
    dev_src = here / "src"
    if (dev_src / PACKAGE_NAME).is_dir():
        return here, dev_src
    release_root = here / RELEASE_FOLDER_NAME
    if (release_root / PACKAGE_NAME).is_dir():
        return release_root, release_root
    return here, here


_HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
_ROOT, _PACKAGE_DIR = resolve_layout(_HERE)
if str(_PACKAGE_DIR) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(_PACKAGE_DIR))

try:
    import idaapi
except ImportError:  # Allows unit tests to import this module outside IDA.
    idaapi = None  # type: ignore[assignment]

from ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin.plugin import PluginController


if idaapi is not None:

    class IdaAiMalwareAnalystPlugin(idaapi.plugin_t):
        flags = idaapi.PLUGIN_KEEP
        comment = "Lightweight native AI assistant foundation for IDA"
        help = "Open the AI Assistant panel from the View menu."
        wanted_name = "IDA AI Malware Analyst"
        wanted_hotkey = ""

        def __init__(self) -> None:
            super().__init__()
            self._controller = PluginController(_ROOT)

        def init(self) -> int:
            return idaapi.PLUGIN_KEEP if self._controller.start() else idaapi.PLUGIN_SKIP

        def run(self, arg: int) -> None:
            del arg
            self._controller.show_assistant()

        def term(self) -> None:
            self._controller.shutdown()


def PLUGIN_ENTRY():
    """IDA's required plugin factory."""
    if idaapi is None:
        return None
    return IdaAiMalwareAnalystPlugin()

27	           https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cli/releases
28	         and put it on PATH (or enter its path in Settings), choose the Claude
29	         provider and click "Sign in with Claude". The CLI opens the browser,
30	         lets you pick the organisation/workspace (SSO supported) and keeps the

33	     Settings are written to ida_ai_malware_analyst/ida_ai_malware_analyst.json
34	     (or the per-user IDA folder). Optional environment overrides:

1	# IDA AI Malware Analyst 1.5.0: changes
2	
3	## Correct verdicts for Go, Rust, Delphi, Nim and C/C++ (wrong "legitimate" for Go malware)
4	
5	Root causes in 1.4.0:
6	
7	1. **Collection cap in address order.** `TriageLimits.max_functions = 5000` and `collect_binary_overview` stopped at the first 5,000 functions by address. Go, Rust and Delphi place the runtime and standard library first and the author's code last. On a 10,000-function Go stealer, the verdict never saw `main.*`.
8	2. **MSVC-only library filter.** Noise detection only knew CRT names, so `runtime.*`, `core::*`, `System::*` and similar were treated as application code.
9	3. **Benign bias for static runtimes.** `high_library_ratio` (-15) rewarded every statically linked binary.
10	4. **Capabilities scored from the IAT only.** Go calls Windows through its own runtime, so its IAT shows nothing. Meanwhile its baseline runtime imports (LoadLibrary, GetProcAddress, SetThreadContext and so on) produced false capability hits.
11	
12	Fixes:
13	
14	- **New `analysis/code_origin.py`:**
15	  - Detects the language (Go, Rust, Delphi, Nim, .NET, C/C++).
16	  - Classifies every function as author, runtime, stdlib, third-party, compiler or thunk, by name with IDA flags and string hints.
17	  - Builds a whole-IDB origin table.
18	  - Safety rules so application code is never skipped:
19	    - Unknown functions are always treated as author code.
20	    - Unnamed helpers count as library only when every caller is a name-recognised static library (never CRT, runtime or FLIRT-only code), so a stripped `main` is never hidden.
21	    - Go modules that `main` calls directly, and that aren't well-known libraries, count as application code (e.g. `github.com/<org>/<implant>`).
22	    - Library-located functions with malicious-behaviour names are kept for analysis.
23	- **`ida/triage_data.py`:** inventories *all* functions (up to 250k) cheaply, then spends the detailed-summary budget on author code first. Every summary carries `origin` and `package`.
24	- **New `analysis/behaviour.py`:** behaviour signals that work without an IAT:
25	  - author function names (stealer, RAT, keylogger, ransomware, loader, PUP and so on)
26	  - high-signal strings (browser stores, wallets, ransom notes, C2 frameworks, browser-hijack keys)
27	  - capability libraries (Go modules, Rust crates)
28	- **`analysis/verdict.py`:**
29	  - Language-aware: runtime baseline APIs are ignored, there's no library-ratio benign bias for static runtimes, and the dynamic-resolution and import-starvation rules are skipped where they're normal.
30	  - Corroborated behaviour evidence, plus score floors for multi-source malware.
31	  - PUP band handling.
32	  - New `classification` (MALWARE / PUP/PUA / SUSPICIOUS-INCONCLUSIVE / LEGITIMATE), `subtype` and `confidence`.
33	- **`analysis/triage.py`:** non-author code is never ranked as interesting (-40). Author functions with behaviour names are ranked up.
34	
35	## Investigate top N
36	- Picks the N functions that **together cover the most capability** (greedy coverage over a 120-function candidate pool), not the first N a depth-first walk reaches.
37	- Results now appear in the **Findings** tab as a concise conclusion: the capabilities found, then one line per function. Chain, path and IOCs stay in the Investigation tab, with no duplicated summary lines.
38	
39	## Report tab (independent and structured)
40	- A new **Report** tab. The report no longer depends on what other tabs left in the history. It re-derives the verdict locally, selects the top author functions, analyses their decompiled code and synthesises the attack chain.
41	- The structure follows a manual analyst report:
42	  1. Verdict (classification, subtype, confidence)
43	  2. Metadata
44	  3. Code origin
45	  4. Ranked findings ([CONFIRMED]/[INFERRED]/[HYPOTHESIS] with addresses)
46	  5. Key author functions
47	  6. Execution flow
48	  7. IOCs (defanged)
49	  8. ATT&CK
50	  9. Packing
51	  10. Alternative hypotheses
52	  11. Limitations
53	  12. Next steps
54	  13. Coverage
55	
56	## Local analysis database (`core/store.py`)
57	- An in-memory SQLite database for the current IDA session (see "Session-scoped local storage" below), keyed by the input file's SHA-256. Uses only the standard-library `sqlite3`.
58	- **Response cache for every tab:** identical requests (same function context, same prompt) are replayed locally at 0 tokens. A renamed, retyped or patched function changes the request and is re-analysed. Responses are stored only after the action succeeded.
59	- **Function records:** every function analysis, sweep analysis or capability result is stored. Report reuses them, and Ask AI answers "what does `<function>` do?" from the database without tokens (prefix `!` to force the model).
60	- **Clear Cache** clears memory and the database rows of the current binary.
61	
62	## Proposed Changes
63	- The list shows only proposals **awaiting a decision**. Approved, rejected and failed items leave immediately; their record stays in History/Audit.
64	- **Show applied changes (for rollback)** reveals applied items when needed.
65	- A new suggestion for the same function supersedes the older pending one, so repeated naming passes don't stack.
66	
67	## Function naming (binary)
68	- Only application code is sent (never runtime, stdlib, third-party or compiler code), most interesting first.
69	- Output is a one-line summary plus the queued names. When nothing is queued, it says why: already pending, not writable, or the model declined for lack of evidence.
70	
71	## Binary Triage: new deterministic checks (no model)
72	- **PE-file facts (`analysis/pe_static.py`).** Read from the input file on disk:
73	  - Authenticode presence and signer (parsed, not verified)
74	  - version info
75	  - exports and internal DLL name
76	  - resources (entropy, magic) and overlay
77	  - .NET, TLS and Rich header
78	- **Wrapper detection,** each with an extraction hint:
79	  - installers and bundlers: Inno, NSIS, AutoIt, PyInstaller, Nuitka, py2exe
80	  - archives: 7z, RAR, ZIP, CAB SFX
81	  - app runtimes: Neutralino, Electron
82	  - packers and protectors: UPX (packed, or marker only), Themida, VMProtect, Enigma
83	- **Side-loading and proxy DLL detection.** A finding needs two or more of these indicators:
84	  - most exports share one stub
85	  - an export points into a high-entropy executable section
86	  - the internal name is a known side-load target, or imitates a vendor (NVIDIA, Microsoft …) while unsigned
87	  - forwarded exports
88	  - DllMain changes page protection in the host module
89	  A corroborated, unsigned side-load scores +20 and sets a 65 floor ("Loader (DLL side-loading)").
90	- **Vendor masquerade:** unsigned file whose version info claims a known vendor (+8).
91	- **Embedded payloads:** a PE inside a resource or the overlay (+10), and ≥2 high-entropy resources with identical first bytes, i.e. encrypted with the same key (+8). Both are informational inside installers.
92	- **Signature as a benign signal** (-10), used only when no malware behaviour or side-loading was corroborated.
93	- **Wrapper and .NET notes,** with reduced confidence for "legitimate": the outer stub isn't the payload.
94	- **Go/Rust/Nim string literal recovery** (`analysis/literal_strings.py`, `ida/literal_reader.py`). Unterminated (pointer, length) literals are rebuilt from `LEA addr` + `MOV len` pairs in author functions. They feed the verdict, behaviour signals and IOCs, so C2 URLs, browser paths and commands in Go malware are now seen.
95	- Results on the analysed samples:
96	  - **Side-loading confirmed:** 0784 and 6BDF; BD0A once DllMain's host patch is seen in IDA
97	  - **Signer:** n8n GmbH (3DD6)
98	  - **Wrappers:** Inno (88BE), Neutralino (500D), UPX marker on the dumped image (F50A)
99	  - **Encrypted same-prefix resources:** 0784 and 6BDF
100	  - **No false positives:** Unity (5C28), CODESYS (95EF)
101	
102	## Binary Triage: code signals, family hints, explainability
103	- **Per-function code signals** (`analysis/code_signals.py`, `ida/code_reader.py`): author code only, bounded to 600 functions / 250k instructions, ranking order.
104	  - **Decoded strings:** stack strings, and single-byte XOR loops whose key and data buffer are visible. They're added to the string pool, so behaviour, IOC and family checks see them.
105	  - **API hashing:** immediates matched against precomputed ROR13 (Metasploit DLL+function), CRC32, DJB2, FNV-1a, SDBM and Murmur3 hashes of the ~900-entry API catalogue. The best algorithm needs ≥2 hits, so a single random constant never resolves. Resolved APIs become `hash:<API>` calls, so the existing injection and hollowing combinations fire on hashed code. Evidence: +15 dynamic resolution.
106	  - **Crypto:** algorithm immediates (TEA, MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256, ChaCha/Salsa, CRC32/32C, Blowfish, RC5/6, MT19937, FNV, Murmur, LCGs, ROR-13 loops) and data tables (AES S-box / inverse S-box / T-table, CRC32 table, Base64 alphabet, Blowfish S-box). Tables are attributed to functions through cross-references. Used for ranking and roles; not scored on their own.
107	  - **Anti-analysis instructions:** `rdtsc`, `cpuid` hypervisor leaf, PEB `BeingDebugged`/`NtGlobalFlag` reads, `int 2Dh`, `icebp`, VMware backdoor port and `VMXh` magic, `sidt`/`sgdt`/`sldt`/`str`, `KUSER_SHARED_DATA`. Scored (+8) only with two or more patterns.
108	  - **Corroborated evasion:** two of {API hashing, anti-analysis instructions, malware family markers} set a 65 floor ("Evasive loader / backdoor").
109	  - A low-score sample with concrete capability evidence is now SUSPICIOUS-INCONCLUSIVE instead of "legitimate".
110	- **Family marker hints** (`analysis/family_markers.py`), offline, no YARA:
111	  - Families covered: Winos4.0/ValleyRAT, Gh0st, Sliver, Cobalt Strike, Meterpreter, Mimikatz, Salat, Kuluoz/Asprox, AsyncRAT/DcRAT, Quasar, Remcos, njRAT, RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Agent Tesla, XMRig, ChromeLoader-style hijackers.
112	  - A hint needs ≥2 markers, or one unique marker.
113	  - Shown as hints, worth +10 (+5 for PUP families), and appended to the subtype ("… — likely Sliver C2 implant").
114	- **Explainability:**
115	  - The verdict prints its confidence breakdown, e.g. `base 60 · score 82/100: +17 · 3 source kinds: +12 · … = 91%`.
116	  - Every evidence address and every function with code signals is in the Triage jump list (double-click to jump).
117	- **Changes since the last triage** (this session): verdict and score changes, evidence added or removed, new top functions, new code signals. Useful after renaming, unpacking or retyping.
118	
119	## Session-scoped local storage
120	- The analysis database is now **in memory for the current IDA session only**. It is cleared when IDA closes the database (plugin `term`) or when a different file is opened, and nothing about the analysed file is written to disk.
121	- A `<idb>.ai_analysis.sqlite` file left by an earlier 1.5 build is deleted automatically.
122	
123	## Less verbose tabs
124	- **Triage:** verdict (evidence listed once), a one-line conclusion, the code-origin table, a packing headline, the top 10 author functions and the top 5 call flows. The full path is in the jump list; the full write-up is in Report.
125

# IDA AI Malware Analyst 1.5.0: changes

## Correct verdicts for Go, Rust, Delphi, Nim and C/C++ (wrong "legitimate" for Go malware)

Root causes in 1.4.0:

1. **Collection cap in address order.** `TriageLimits.max_functions = 5000` and `collect_binary_overview` stopped at the first 5,000 functions by address. Go, Rust and Delphi place the runtime and standard library first and the author's code last. On a 10,000-function Go stealer, the verdict never saw `main.*`.
2. **MSVC-only library filter.** Noise detection only knew CRT names, so `runtime.*`, `core::*`, `System::*` and similar were treated as application code.
3. **Benign bias for static runtimes.** `high_library_ratio` (-15) rewarded every statically linked binary.
4. **Capabilities scored from the IAT only.** Go calls Windows through its own runtime, so its IAT shows nothing. Meanwhile its baseline runtime imports (LoadLibrary, GetProcAddress, SetThreadContext and so on) produced false capability hits.

Fixes:

- **New `analysis/code_origin.py`:**
  - Detects the language (Go, Rust, Delphi, Nim, .NET, C/C++).
  - Classifies every function as author, runtime, stdlib, third-party, compiler or thunk, by name with IDA flags and string hints.
  - Builds a whole-IDB origin table.
  - Safety rules so application code is never skipped:
    - Unknown functions are always treated as author code.
    - Unnamed helpers count as library only when every caller is a name-recognised static library (never CRT, runtime or FLIRT-only code), so a stripped `main` is never hidden.
    - Go modules that `main` calls directly, and that aren't well-known libraries, count as application code (e.g. `github.com/<org>/<implant>`).
    - Library-located functions with malicious-behaviour names are kept for analysis.
- **`ida/triage_data.py`:** inventories *all* functions (up to 250k) cheaply, then spends the detailed-summary budget on author code first. Every summary carries `origin` and `package`.
- **New `analysis/behaviour.py`:** behaviour signals that work without an IAT:
  - author function names (stealer, RAT, keylogger, ransomware, loader, PUP and so on)
  - high-signal strings (browser stores, wallets, ransom notes, C2 frameworks, browser-hijack keys)
  - capability libraries (Go modules, Rust crates)
- **`analysis/verdict.py`:**
  - Language-aware: runtime baseline APIs are ignored, there's no library-ratio benign bias for static runtimes, and the dynamic-resolution and import-starvation rules are skipped where they're normal.
  - Corroborated behaviour evidence, plus score floors for multi-source malware.
  - PUP band handling.
  - New `classification` (MALWARE / PUP/PUA / SUSPICIOUS-INCONCLUSIVE / LEGITIMATE), `subtype` and `confidence`.
- **`analysis/triage.py`:** non-author code is never ranked as interesting (-40). Author functions with behaviour names are ranked up.

## Investigate top N
- Picks the N functions that **together cover the most capability** (greedy coverage over a 120-function candidate pool), not the first N a depth-first walk reaches.
- Results now appear in the **Findings** tab as a concise conclusion: the capabilities found, then one line per function. Chain, path and IOCs stay in the Investigation tab, with no duplicated summary lines.

## Report tab (independent and structured)
- A new **Report** tab. The report no longer depends on what other tabs left in the history. It re-derives the verdict locally, selects the top author functions, analyses their decompiled code and synthesises the attack chain.
- The structure follows a manual analyst report:
  1. Verdict (classification, subtype, confidence)
  2. Metadata
  3. Code origin
  4. Ranked findings ([CONFIRMED]/[INFERRED]/[HYPOTHESIS] with addresses)
  5. Key author functions
  6. Execution flow
  7. IOCs (defanged)
  8. ATT&CK
  9. Packing
  10. Alternative hypotheses
  11. Limitations
  12. Next steps
  13. Coverage

## Local analysis database (`core/store.py`)
- An in-memory SQLite database for the current IDA session (see "Session-scoped local storage" below), keyed by the input file's SHA-256. Uses only the standard-library `sqlite3`.
- **Response cache for every tab:** identical requests (same function context, same prompt) are replayed locally at 0 tokens. A renamed, retyped or patched function changes the request and is re-analysed. Responses are stored only after the action succeeded.
- **Function records:** every function analysis, sweep analysis or capability result is stored. Report reuses them, and Ask AI answers "what does `<function>` do?" from the database without tokens (prefix `!` to force the model).
- **Clear Cache** clears memory and the database rows of the current binary.

## Proposed Changes
- The list shows only proposals **awaiting a decision**. Approved, rejected and failed items leave immediately; their record stays in History/Audit.
- **Show applied changes (for rollback)** reveals applied items when needed.
- A new suggestion for the same function supersedes the older pending one, so repeated naming passes don't stack.

## Function naming (binary)
- Only application code is sent (never runtime, stdlib, third-party or compiler code), most interesting first.
- Output is a one-line summary plus the queued names. When nothing is queued, it says why: already pending, not writable, or the model declined for lack of evidence.

## Binary Triage: new deterministic checks (no model)
- **PE-file facts (`analysis/pe_static.py`).** Read from the input file on disk:
  - Authenticode presence and signer (parsed, not verified)
  - version info
  - exports and internal DLL name
  - resources (entropy, magic) and overlay
  - .NET, TLS and Rich header
- **Wrapper detection,** each with an extraction hint:
  - installers and bundlers: Inno, NSIS, AutoIt, PyInstaller, Nuitka, py2exe
  - archives: 7z, RAR, ZIP, CAB SFX
  - app runtimes: Neutralino, Electron
  - packers and protectors: UPX (packed, or marker only), Themida, VMProtect, Enigma
- **Side-loading and proxy DLL detection.** A finding needs two or more of these indicators:
  - most exports share one stub
  - an export points into a high-entropy executable section
  - the internal name is a known side-load target, or imitates a vendor (NVIDIA, Microsoft …) while unsigned
  - forwarded exports
  - DllMain changes page protection in the host module

- **Wrapper and .NET notes,** with reduced confidence for "legitimate": the outer stub isn't the payload.
- **Go/Rust/Nim string literal recovery** (`analysis/literal_strings.py`, `ida/literal_reader.py`). Unterminated (pointer, length) literals are rebuilt from `LEA addr` + `MOV len` pairs in author functions. They feed the verdict, behaviour signals and IOCs, so C2 URLs, browser paths and commands in Go malware are now seen.
- Results on the analysed samples:
  - **Side-loading confirmed:** 0784 and 6BDF; BD0A once DllMain's host patch is seen in IDA
  - **Signer:** n8n GmbH (3DD6)
  - **Wrappers:** Inno (88BE), Neutralino (500D), UPX marker on the dumped image (F50A)
  - **Encrypted same-prefix resources:** 0784 and 6BDF
  - **No false positives:** Unity (5C28), CODESYS (95EF)

## Binary Triage: code signals, family hints, explainability
- **Per-function code signals** (`analysis/code_signals.py`, `ida/code_reader.py`): author code only, bounded to 600 functions / 250k instructions, ranking order.

  - **API hashing:** immediates matched against precomputed ROR13 (Metasploit DLL+function), CRC32, DJB2, FNV-1a, SDBM and Murmur3 hashes of the ~900-entry API catalogue. The best algorithm needs ≥2 hits, so a single random constant never resolves. Resolved APIs become `hash:<API>` calls, so the existing injection and hollowing combinations fire on hashed code. Evidence: +15 dynamic resolution.
  - **Crypto:** algorithm immediates (TEA, MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256, ChaCha/Salsa, CRC32/32C, Blowfish, RC5/6, MT19937, FNV, Murmur, LCGs, ROR-13 loops) and data tables (AES S-box / inverse S-box / T-table, CRC32 table, Base64 alphabet, Blowfish S-box). Tables are attributed to functions through cross-references. Used for ranking and roles; not scored on their own.
  - **Anti-analysis instructions:** `rdtsc`, `cpuid` hypervisor leaf, PEB `BeingDebugged`/`NtGlobalFlag` reads, `int 2Dh`, `icebp`, VMware backdoor port and `VMXh` magic, `sidt`/`sgdt`/`sldt`/`str`, `KUSER_SHARED_DATA`. Scored (+8) only with two or more patterns.

  - A hint needs ≥2 markers, or one unique marker.
  - Shown as hints, worth +10 (+5 for PUP families), and appended to the subtype ("… — likely Sliver C2 implant").
- **Explainability:**
  - The verdict prints its confidence breakdown, e.g. `base 60 · score 82/100: +17 · 3 source kinds: +12 · … = 91%`.
  - Every evidence address and every function with code signals is in the Triage jump list (double-click to jump).
- **Changes since the last triage** (this session): verdict and score changes, evidence added or removed, new top functions, new code signals. Useful after renaming, unpacking or retyping.

## Session-scoped local storage
- The analysis database is now **in memory for the current IDA session only**. It is cleared when IDA closes the database (plugin `term`) or when a different file is opened, and nothing about the analysed file is written to disk.
- A `<idb>.ai_analysis.sqlite` file left by an earlier 1.5 build is deleted automatically.

## Less verbose tabs
- **Triage:** verdict (evidence listed once), a one-line conclusion, the code-origin table, a packing headline, the top 10 author functions and the top 5 call flows. The full path is in the jump list; the full write-up is in Report.

## Sign-in only (no API keys)
- Two providers, both browser sign-in. API-key, Gemini and OpenAI-compatible providers are removed (`llm/gemini.py`, `llm/openai_compat.py`).
  - **ChatGPT:** OAuth PKCE on a loopback port (127.0.0.1:1455). Your credentials are typed only into the OpenAI page in your browser; the plugin never sees them, and the callback is checked against a random `state`.
  - **Claude:** Anthropic's official CLI (`ant auth login`), with organisation SSO. The plugin asks the CLI for a short-lived access token and keeps it in memory only.
- **Session-only tokens by default.** ChatGPT tokens stay in memory and are revoked when IDA closes. "Remember ChatGPT sign-in" (off by default) stores them DPAPI-protected instead.
- "Cancel sign-in", "Copy link" (when no browser opens), "Disconnect" (revoke and remove) and "Forget account".
- Old configuration files still load. Their API-key, base-URL and Gemini fields are ignored and dropped on the next save; `gemini_timeout_seconds` and `gemini_max_retries` carry over as `request_timeout_seconds` and `max_retries`.
- Claude requests follow the current API: no assistant prefill and no `temperature` (Claude 5 models reject both), `max_tokens` of at least 16,000, default model `claude-opus-5-5`, and server-side fallback to the default model.
- Transport: POST requests aren't retried at the socket level (no duplicate billing). 429 and 5xx responses are retried with `Retry-After` and jitter.

## Production hardening
- **Report safety:** sample-derived names, strings and model text are Markdown-escaped or put in inline code, so a crafted string can't inject links, headings or tables. Reports are capped at 512 KiB.
- **Panel:**
  - Buttons are grouped into a *Binary* row (Binary Triage, Report, Cancel, Settings) and a *Function* row (Analyze, Investigate, Suggest Names, Capabilities, Obfuscation, Rename…, Comment…). Every button has a tooltip.
  - While an action runs, the action buttons are disabled, and a progress indicator and elapsed timer are shown.
  - The Report tab renders Markdown (links are inert). It has "Show raw Markdown" and "Copy Markdown".
  - Monospace, non-wrapping text for triage, call flows, the trace and history.
  - Proposed Changes: the tab caption shows the pending count. Hover a change to see its full values, reason, evidence and confidence; double-click to jump to it. Approve All and Rollback ask for confirmation.
  - A result no longer pulls you away from the tab you moved to while it ran; its tab is highlighted instead.
  - The trace gets a separator for each run. Status lines use the button names. Settings errors show the error message, not just its type.
  - Ask AI keeps the conversation and has a Clear button.
- **Cleanup:**
  - The superseded history-based report generator is removed (`analysis/report.py` went from 1,100 to 270 lines).
  - Removed the orphaned 1.4 function-analysis callbacks, the API-key leftovers and unused imports.
  - Line endings are LF throughout.
- **Tests and release:**
  - `tests/run_tests.py` runs 8 offline suites: verdict, pipeline, collection, triage, code signals, PE facts, sign-in and UI helpers. They need no IDA, network or model. Real-sample checks run only when `IDA_AI_SAMPLES_DIR` points at read-only sample copies.
  - `scripts/build_release.py` builds `dist/ida_ai_malware_analyst-<version>.zip` after three gates: everything compiles, the tests pass, and the package contains no API keys, tokens, local configuration, user paths or e-mail addresses.

# IDA AI Malware Analyst 1.5: user guide

A lightweight IDA Pro panel for static, analyst-controlled malware triage. The deterministic parts (verdict, code origin, PE facts, code signals) run locally and cost no tokens. AI actions run only when you click them. Nothing is written to the IDB until you approve it.

## 1. Sign in

Open **Settings** and choose a provider:

| Provider | How you sign in | Where the tokens live |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ChatGPT (default) | **Sign in with ChatGPT** opens the OpenAI page in your browser. | In memory for this IDA session, revoked on exit. Tick **Remember ChatGPT sign-in** to keep them, DPAPI-protected. |
| Claude | **Sign in with Claude** runs Anthropic's CLI (`ant`), which opens the browser. Organisation SSO is supported. | With the Anthropic CLI. The plugin holds only a short-lived access token in memory. |

You type your password only into the provider's own page, never into IDA.

If no browser opens, use **Copy link**. **Cancel sign-in** stops a sign-in that is waiting for the browser. **Disconnect** revokes the session and removes it.

## 2. Recommended workflow

1. **Binary Triage** (no tokens) gives:
   - the classification (MALWARE, PUP/PUA, SUSPICIOUS-INCONCLUSIVE or LEGITIMATE) with subtype and confidence breakdown
   - the code-origin table (author code vs runtime, stdlib, third-party and compiler code)
   - static PE facts and code signals
   - the top author functions

   Double-click any row in the jump list to go to that address.
2. **Investigate top N** (Triage tab) runs AI analysis of the N author functions that together cover the most capability. Results go to **Findings**, and chain, path and IOCs go to **Investigation**.
3. **Report** builds the structured whole-binary report: verdict, metadata, origin, ranked findings, key functions, execution flow, IOCs, ATT&CK, packing, alternatives, limitations, next steps and coverage. It reuses every analysis already done this session, so only missing functions cost tokens. It is saved as Markdown next to the IDB.
4. Drill into single functions with the Function row: Analyze, Investigate, Capabilities, Obfuscation or Suggest Names.
5. Review **Proposed Changes**:
   - Hover a change for its reason and evidence.
   - Double-click a change to jump to it.
   - Approve the changes you want. Every applied change can be rolled back.

## 3. What is filtered and what never is

- Runtime, standard-library, third-party and compiler-generated functions are recognised by name, IDA flags and language (Go, Rust, Delphi, Nim, .NET, C/C++). They are skipped for AI analysis.
- **Application code is never skipped:**
  - Unknown functions count as author code.
  - Unnamed helpers count as library code only when every caller is a name-recognised static library.
  - Go modules that `main` calls directly count as application code.
  - Library-located functions with malicious-behaviour names are kept.

## 4. Tabs

| Tab | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Findings | Result of the last function action, or the Investigate-top-N conclusion |
| Report | Rendered report; *Show raw Markdown*, *Copy Markdown* |
| Proposed Changes (N) | Pending IDB edits; *Show applied changes* to roll back |
| Investigation | Attack chain, analysis path (jump list), defanged indicators, trace |
| Triage | Deterministic triage, *Investigate top N*, *Suggest Names (Binary)* |
| Obfuscation | Packing assessment, decoded artifacts, *Propose comments*, *Copy Python* (review-only, never run) |
| History | Everything done this session; *Clear Cache* |
| Ask AI | Questions about the current function or stored results. Prefix `!` to force a fresh model answer. |

While an action runs, the action buttons are disabled and an elapsed timer is shown; **Cancel** stops the action after its current step. If you switch tabs while an action runs, the panel stays where you are and highlights the result tab.

## 5. Privacy and data handling

- **Sent to the provider** only when you click an AI action: bounded context for the selected functions (assembly, pseudocode, strings, names, cross-references) and triage summaries.
- **Analysis cache:** an in-memory database for the current IDA session. It is cleared when the database closes or another file is opened, and nothing about the sample is written to disk except the reports you generate.
- **Static analysis only:** the plugin never runs the sample or any decoded artifact.

IDA AI Malware Analyst 1.5.0
=================================

Lightweight native IDA Pro plugin for analyst-controlled, AI-assisted malware
analysis. Sign-in only - no API keys:
  * ChatGPT  - Sign in with ChatGPT in your browser (uses your ChatGPT plan)
  * Claude   - Sign in with Claude in your browser through Anthropic's official
               CLI (organisation SSO supported; billed to that Console org)
No pip install, virtual environment or SDK needed.

INSTALL
  1. Copy BOTH of these into IDA's plugins directory:
       ida_ai_malware_analyst.py
       ida_ai_malware_analyst/        (the whole folder)
     Plugins directory:
       Windows  %APPDATA%\Hex-Rays\IDA Pro\plugins   (or <IDA install>\plugins)
       Linux    ~/.idapro/plugins                     (or <IDA install>/plugins)
       macOS    ~/.idapro/plugins                     (or <IDA.app>/Contents/MacOS/plugins)
  2. Restart IDA, open a database and use View -> Open subviews -> AI Assistant
     or Edit -> Plugins -> AI Analyst.
  3. In the panel click Settings:
       ChatGPT (default): click "Sign in with ChatGPT" and finish in the browser.
         If no browser opens, use "Copy link" and paste it into a browser.
         "Disconnect" revokes and removes the session; "Forget account" also
         removes the registration (needed to switch ChatGPT accounts).
       Claude: install the Anthropic CLI (ant) from
           https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cli/releases
         and put it on PATH (or enter its path in Settings), choose the Claude
         provider and click "Sign in with Claude". The CLI opens the browser,
         lets you pick the organisation/workspace (SSO supported) and keeps the
         sign-in in %APPDATA%\Anthropic. Usage is billed to that organisation.
       "Cancel sign-in" stops a sign-in that is waiting for the browser.
     Settings are written to ida_ai_malware_analyst/ida_ai_malware_analyst.json
     (or the per-user IDA folder). Optional environment overrides:
       IDA_AI_PROVIDER=chatgpt|claude   IDA_AI_MODEL=<model id>
     Configuration files from older versions still load; their API-key and
     base-URL fields are ignored and removed on the next save.

REQUIREMENTS
  IDA Pro 9.x with IDAPython on Python 3.9 or newer. Hex-Rays is optional.
  ChatGPT sign-in needs a browser and network access to auth.openai.com and
  api.openai.com; it is available to eligible plans and subject to plan limits.
  Claude sign-in needs the Anthropic CLI and access to api.anthropic.com.

DATA HANDLING
  Bounded context for the function you analyse (assembly, pseudocode, strings,
  names, cross-references) and whole-binary triage summaries are sent to the
  provider you signed in to (ChatGPT or Claude) when you click an AI action.
  ChatGPT tokens are stored in the per-user IDA profile, protected with Windows
  DPAPI (owner-only file permissions on POSIX). Claude tokens stay with the
  Anthropic CLI; the plugin only keeps a short-lived access token in memory.
  Analysis results are cached in memory for the current IDA session only and
  are discarded when IDA closes the database. Nothing is sent without an
  analyst action and nothing is written to the IDB without explicit approval.

UNINSTALL
  Delete ida_ai_malware_analyst.py and the ida_ai_malware_analyst/ folder from plugins/.

- **Sent to the provider** only when you click an AI action: bounded context for the selected functions (assembly, pseudocode, strings, names, cross-references) and triage summaries.
- **Analysis cache:** an in-memory database for the current IDA session. It is cleared when the database closes or another file is opened, and nothing about the sample is written to disk except the reports you generate.
- **Static analysis only:** the plugin never runs the sample or any decoded artifact.

"""IDA entry point for the IDA AI Malware Analyst plugin.

This file is the only module IDA loads from its ``plugins`` directory. It
locates the plugin package and support files in one of two layouts and has no
AI or network behaviour of its own.

Release layout (what ``scripts/build_release.py`` produces and what an analyst
copies into IDA's ``plugins`` directory)::

    plugins/
      ida_ai_malware_analyst.py                 <- this file
      ida_ai_malware_analyst/                   <- plugin root
        ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin/          <- the package
        prompts/
        ida_ai_malware_analyst.json             <- optional local configuration

Development layout (this repository)::

    <repo>/
      ida_ai_malware_analyst.py                 <- this file; repo root is the plugin root
      src/ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin/
      prompts/
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Tuple


RELEASE_FOLDER_NAME = "ida_ai_malware_analyst"
PACKAGE_NAME = "ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin"


def resolve_layout(here: Path) -> Tuple[Path, Path]:
    """Return ``(plugin_root, package_dir)`` for the directory containing this file.

    ``plugin_root`` holds ``prompts/`` and the optional configuration file;
    ``package_dir`` is the ``sys.path`` entry that contains the package.
    Candidates, in order: the development layout (``<here>/src``), then the
    release layout (``<here>/ida_ai_malware_analyst/``). When neither exists the
    directory itself is used so a flat copy still imports.
    """
    dev_src = here / "src"
    if (dev_src / PACKAGE_NAME).is_dir():
        return here, dev_src
    release_root = here / RELEASE_FOLDER_NAME
    if (release_root / PACKAGE_NAME).is_dir():
        return release_root, release_root
    return here, here


_HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
_ROOT, _PACKAGE_DIR = resolve_layout(_HERE)
if str(_PACKAGE_DIR) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(_PACKAGE_DIR))

try:
    import idaapi
except ImportError:  # Allows unit tests to import this module outside IDA.
    idaapi = None  # type: ignore[assignment]

from ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin.plugin import PluginController


if idaapi is not None:

    class IdaAiMalwareAnalystPlugin(idaapi.plugin_t):
        flags = idaapi.PLUGIN_KEEP
        comment = "Lightweight native AI assistant foundation for IDA"
        help = "Open the AI Assistant panel from the View menu."
        wanted_name = "IDA AI Malware Analyst"
        wanted_hotkey = ""

        def __init__(self) -> None:
            super().__init__()
            self._controller = PluginController(_ROOT)

        def init(self) -> int:
            return idaapi.PLUGIN_KEEP if self._controller.start() else idaapi.PLUGIN_SKIP

        def run(self, arg: int) -> None:
            del arg
            self._controller.show_assistant()

        def term(self) -> None:
            self._controller.shutdown()


def PLUGIN_ENTRY():
    """IDA's required plugin factory."""
    if idaapi is None:
        return None
    return IdaAiMalwareAnalystPlugin()

The plugin is in a releasable state. All 8 offline test suites pass, the real-sample checks pass on your sample copies, and the release zip builds cleanly. One gap: the new panel code has not been run inside IDA, because there is no PyQt5 on this box. It compiles and its helper functions are tested, but please do the quick in-IDA check at the end before you ship.

**1. Report safety**
- Names, strings and model text taken from the sample are now escaped in the report, so a crafted string in a binary can't inject links, headings or tables.
- Reports are capped at 512 KiB.
- Ask AI keeps the conversation and has a Clear button.

**2. Panel**
- **Layout:** buttons are split into a **Binary** row (Binary Triage, Report, Cancel, Settings) and a **Function** row (Analyze, Investigate, Suggest Names, Capabilities, Obfuscation, Rename…, Comment…). Every button has a tooltip.
- **While an action runs:** the action buttons are disabled and a progress bar with an elapsed timer is shown, so you can't start two actions at once.
- **Report tab:** shows formatted Markdown (links don't open), with "Show raw Markdown" and "Copy Markdown".
- **Text:** Triage, flows, trace and history use a fixed-width font without line wrapping.
- **Proposed Changes:**
  - The tab title shows the pending count, e.g. "Proposed Changes (5)".
  - Hovering a change shows its full values, reason, evidence and confidence; double-clicking jumps to its address.
  - Approve All and Rollback now ask for confirmation.
- **Tab switching:** if you move to another tab while an action runs, the result no longer pulls you away; its tab is highlighted instead.
- Each run gets a separator in the trace, and errors now show the actual message.

**3. Cleanup**
- `analysis/report.py` went from about 1,100 to 270 lines; the old history-based report generator it held was no longer used.
- Removed the unused 1.4 analysis callbacks, the API-key leftovers and unused imports in 14 files.

**4. Tests, release build and docs**
- **Tests:** `tests\run_tests.py` runs everything offline (no IDA, network or model). The real-sample checks are skipped unless `IDA_AI_SAMPLES_DIR` points at your sample copies, so the repo contains no paths to malware.
- **Release build:** `scripts\build_release.py` only produces the zip if everything compiles, the tests pass, and the package contains no API keys, tokens, local config, user paths or e-mail addresses. Today's output is `dist\ida_ai_malware_analyst-1.5.0.zip` (79 files). It is a plain zip; encrypt it yourself if you keep publishing it password-protected on GitHub.
- **Docs:**

  - `CHANGELOG-1.5.0.md` now covers sign-in and this hardening work.
  - I fixed `README-INSTALL.txt`, which still said ChatGPT tokens are saved to disk. They are now kept in memory for the session and revoked on exit, unless you tick "Remember".
- **Old guide left out:** the v1.4.0 complete guide still describes API-key and Gemini sign-in, so the release no longer includes it. Your local copy is untouched.
